idiom_name: defined type with unexported storage (type Orders struct{ items []Order }) + slices.Clone at the edges
implementation_notes: Go's type system gives collection syntax to any defined type: len, range, indexing and slicing work on a named type over []Order, so only the domain methods have to be written and the classic 'wrapper class that implements the collection interface' disappears. Invariant ownership, though, requires the slice to be unexported - a bare type Orders []Order shares its backing array with whatever was passed in, so a caller can still mutate behind the owner's back. Keep the field unexported in a struct, clone at both boundaries (slices.Clone on ingest, and again in any All()/Values() accessor) and return []Order copies rather than the internal slice; the slices package supplies the generic work - append/insert/delete, sorting, compacting.
pitfalls: A defined slice type is still a slice: constructing Orders from a slice aliases the same backing array, so the invariant can be broken through the original; clone on ingest.
append writes into spare capacity that may be shared with another slice (a sub-slice, or a second value copied by assignment); never build the type from an untrusted sub-slice.
Returning the internal slice from an accessor hands out write access to the owner's storage; return a clone or an iterator.
Copying the struct copies the slice header, not the elements: two values then share storage unless every mutator appends into a private array.
